title: Diverse Mock Juries
text:
Psychologist Samuel Sommers of Tufts University wanted to know how the racial makeup of a jury affects its deliberations. He worked with real jury pools in Michigan, recruiting people who had been called for jury duty to take part in mock trials.

Each six-person mock jury watched a video summary of a sexual assault trial with a Black defendant. Some juries were made up entirely of white jurors. Others included four white and two Black jurors. The juries then deliberated, and their discussions were recorded and carefully analyzed.

The racially diverse juries deliberated longer, discussed more of the facts of the case, and made fewer factual mistakes. They were also more willing to talk about difficult issues, such as the role of race in the case.

Strikingly, much of the difference came from the white jurors themselves. White jurors on diverse juries mentioned more case facts and made fewer errors than white jurors on all-white juries, and they were less likely to think the defendant guilty even before the discussion began. Simply knowing they would deliberate with a more diverse group seemed to make them think more carefully.
lesson: Diversity improves a group's thinking partly by changing how the majority thinks. Expecting different perspectives makes people prepare and reason more carefully.
source: Sommers, S. R. (2006). On racial diversity and group decision making: Identifying multiple effects of racial composition on jury deliberations. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 90(4), 597-612.
